headline: Committee carries on with residential parking pilot program and defers stop sign ordinance O-26-024 at French Street and Abbott Street.
summary: The Committee on Infrastructure heard an update on the Residential Parking "Pilot" Program and voted to continue monitoring it. Ordinance O-26-024, authorizing additional stop signs at French Street and Abbott Street, was deferred until the next meeting. Two ordinances on camping and camper/RV prohibitions remained tabled in committee, as did a petition for L Deerwood Drive - Lot H-103.
decisions: Recommended that the committee carry on with the Residential Parking Pilot Program and report back with progress.
Deferred Ordinance O-26-024, authorizing additional stop signs at French Street and Abbott Street, until the next meeting.

TO Jill Stansfield FROM Andrew Hill
COMPANY City of Nashua DATE September 22, 2026
RE Resident Area Parking Permit (RAPP)
Pilot PROJECT NO 26025794_01
CC Liz Hannum PROJECT
NAME Nashua Parking Management
At the request of the client (“Nashua” or “the City”), Thornton Tomasetti (“TT”) was asked to
evaluate the area surrounding the “Property Possible” development as the site of pilot program
to introduce a Resident Parking Permit (RPP) program. The area being evaluated was defined
as shown in the figure below and bounded by Spruce Street to the west, Temple Street to the
north, Commercial Street to the east, and East Hollis Street to the south.
Figure 1: Proposed Pilot Area
The “Property Possible” project is a proposed redevelopment of the former William’s Foundry/J.F.
McElwain Shoe Company factory located at 103 Temple Street, converting the 254,122 square
foot parcel into three multi-family residential buildings providing 385 units and 450 parking spaces.
This program envisions providing parking onsite for residents and their guests at a rate of 1.17
spaces per unit, which is compliant with the recently passed New Hampshire House Bill 1588-FN
which mandates the maximum parking requirement a New Hampshire municipality may impose
on new residential development by local zoning is 1.00 spaces per unit.
Re: Resident Area Parking Permit (RAPP) Pilot             Page 2
Memorandum
Review of actual provided parking for existing residential properties within the proposed pilot area
indicates that existing residential properties are provided roughly 1.60 parking spaces per unit
and utilize, on average, 1.50 spaces per unit under peak demand conditions. In engaging TT, one
of the challenges set forth by the City was to estimate the capacity of the surrounding area to
accommodate potential overflow from the proposed development.
A secondary challenge was to envision a formal Resident Parking Permit (RPP) program, based
on parking management industry best practices, which could be tested and – if successful – serve
as model for overhauling the City’s existing Overnight Parking program.
The City’s Overnight Parking program has been developed in piecemeal fashion, historically in
reaction to community outcry to allow parking along particular roadways on an as-needed basis.
Currently, the city makes up to 550 permits available each year to qualifying citizens 1, allowing
them to park on portions of thirty-three public streets more than the universal time limit of two
hours maximum stay between the hours of midnight (12:00 AM) and 6:00 AM. While reasonably
effective to date, the City would like to replace this program with an alternative program which
can easily be duplicated in other parts of the City as the community demands in a more systematic
fashion.
Pilot Area Parking Supply
To establish the current on-street parking capacity for the pilot area, TT performed an analysis of
existing parking regulations, roadway and sidewalk dimensions, traffic flow, and vehicular turning
movements across both sides of the following public roadways contained within the pilot area:
 Spruce Street, between East Hollis Street and Temple Street.
 Temple Street, between Spruce Street and Commercial Street.
 Commercial Street, between Temple Street and the defunct railroad trestle.
 Hudson Street, from the Nashua Fire Station to East Hollis Street.
 Howard Street, from Spruce Street to Hoyts Lane.
 Worcester Street, from Scripture Street to Shedds Avenue.
 Shedds Avenue, from Worcester Street to Hoyts Lane.
In each case, TT took a measure of the street’s width to determine if it could support parallel
parking along one or both curbs, assuming the provision of one 11’ wide travel lane for each
direction of travel and 9’ wide parking lanes. Applying these dimensions, no roadway with less
than 20’ of clearance from edge to edge could be considered for parallel parking2. Streets greater
than 20’ clear between edges or curbs could support one-way traffic and one parking lane. Streets
with 29’ or more of clearance could support a parking lane along each side, provided traffic flow
along the road was one-way only. Streets with 31’ or more clearance could support two-way
1 Only Nashua citizens living on particular streets, or at particular addresses, can apply for an Overnight
Parking Permit and they must prove residency and limit the use of the permit to legally registered private,
non-commercial, and non-recreational motor vehicles.
2 This eliminated Gorman Street, Scripture Street, and Hoyts Lane from consideration as roadways which
might support parallel parking. TT also did not consider East Hollis Street viable for parallel parking as it
supports one travel lane in each direction as well as central turn lane, taking up almost all of the clear width
of the roadway.
Re: Resident Area Parking Permit (RAPP) Pilot             Page 3
Memorandum
traffic, but only one parking lane. To have two-way traffic and parking lanes along both sides of
the roadway, the street must be at least 40’ wide.
Estimating the parking capacity along each street required identifying minimum required setbacks
from intersections3, fire hydrants 4, driveways5, and other curb cuts along each side of the street
which could support parking and the estimating the parking capacity in each strip of contiguous
curb. For this, TT assumed a distance of 20’ of uninterrupted linear space was equivalent to one
parallel parking space6.
NOTE: While capacity was estimated on a per space basis, TT recommends striping of ‘lanes’
where parallel parking is authorized rather than individual parallel parking stalls. Marking off
individual spaces to accommodate ‘design vehicle’ dimensions often results in inefficient use of
the available parking area when smaller vehicles occupy these spaces. For example, a mid-size
sedan may only require 15 feet in length to park, resulting in five linear feet of unoccupied space.
In string of three contiguous parallel parking spaces, it would be possible to park four mid-sized
sedans in the same space marked to accommodate three ‘design’ vehicles.
Based on this methodology, TT estimates that streets identified can accommodate parking as
follows:

Proposed Permit Distribution Models
As the preceding analysis shows, there is not enough on-street parking supply within the pilot
area to guarantee one parking permit for each residential unit; this would equate to 513 permits
for only 152 spaces or 3.375 permits per available on-street space. This does not necessarily
prohibit the city from granting one permit for each household.
When municipalities allow the issuance of significantly 10 more permits than there are parking
spaces, the are essentially distributing “hunting licenses” to permit holders. Under this model,
the permit does not promise each holder will be able to find a parking space but rather extends
them the right to search for and use a permit only parking space if they can find an open one. The
hunting license model is popular politically because it offers every qualifying permit holder the
right to park in the permit zone, which is perceived as fair and egalitarian. In actual practice, the
hunting license model favors those permit holders with the flexibility to search for open parking
on the days and/or times when occupancy levels are the lowest and, once a vehicle is parked,
the ability to not move their vehicles for extended periods.
If a municipality desires to offer a permit program that aligns the number of available spaces
(“supply”) with the number of issued permits (“demand”), they adopt either a prescription or a
lottery model. A prescription model is based on the equitable 11, rather than egalitarian,
distribution of parking permits. Prescription models factor in the balance between parking supply
and demand within a permit zone. A lottery model can be equitable or egalitarian, depending on
how it is structured.
10 In this case, significantly equates to 10% or more permits than parking spaces, although some
municipalities have reported issuing up to 40% more permits than parking spaces and still recording
utilization rates of less than 100% of available capacity. The concept of selling more permits than parking
spaces is commonly referred to as “oversell” in the parking industry. “Oversell” reflects the difference
between the number of permits issued and the number of permitted vehicles parked at any given time at the
peak hour. As a general rule, a permit program administrator can safely assume up to 10% of all permit
holders will be absent in the permit zone at any given time due to travel, vacations, etc. “Oversell” for a
particular area can only be accurately defined through a program of study conducted across a reasonable
period of time to capture all reasonably anticipated conditions.
11 Equitable is defined as “fair and just in a way that takes account of and seeks to address existing
inequalities” versusegalitarian (“related to or believing in the principle that all people are equal and deserve
equal rights and opportunities”.)

Under a prescription model, the municipality can function as the arbiter of permit rights by
executing a formal property-by-property inventory of household units and off-street parking
supply. This inventory serves as the basis for determining which households can apply for a
parking permit by identifying which properties lack adequate provided off-street parking to support
the number of households contained therein. Under such a model, any household within the
permit zone can apply for a parking permit, but only those households identified as having a valid
need with be issued a permit. In some cases, the municipality may request applicants include a
recommendation from the property owner attesting to the applicant’s need.
Under an open lottery model, any household within the permit zone can apply for a permit and
the municipality randomly selects applications and issues permits up the number of available
permit spaces. Using a limited lottery approach, the municipality imposes criteria which narrows
which households can apply for a permit 12 and then randomly selects and awards permits from
the reduced pool.
None of these models incorporate the impact of permit pricing, which can influence demand for
parking permits. For municipalities seeking to reduce the number of permit applicants overall to
better align with the number of available parking spaces without going to a prescription model,
setting the price per permit can create a ‘self-regulating’ program. Some municipalities have
adopted an escalating scale of permit pricing which makes the first permit affordable, but charges
increasing premiums for each additional permit. A few municipalities have offered parking permits
at different price points according to the applicant’s reported income and/or type of residence
(e.g., rental versus owned, single-family home versus multi-unit complex, etc.).
Of course, all of these models have their detractors. Municipalities which issue hunting licenses
are often subject to criticism by the permit holders who cannot regularly find an open space.
Prescription and limited lottery models are perceived as inherently prejudicial against the property
types or residents that don’t meet criteria. Detractors of the open lottery model argue the process
is too random and does not address specific needs and challenges within the permit zone. And
influencing demand through pricing is perceived as unfair to individuals with restricted incomes
and/or those living in the type of residence not favored by the program design.
No model is considered superior to the others or more preferrable to one kind of municipality.
Model selection is generally reflective of the values and dynamics of each individual community.
For example, Boston, its abutting municipalities, and most other eastern Massachusetts
municipalities have very limited on-street parking supply, tremendous residential density, and
access to transit and other alternative transportation modes; all of these communities elect the
egalitarian hunting license model for their residential parking permit programs. The New
Hampshire municipalities that currently maintain residential parking permit programs tend to be
more prescriptive, although they rely on geography, rather than a qualification of need, to
determine to whom to award a permit. The City of Asbury Park (NJ) follows a classic prescriptive
model that incorporates an assessment of available parking by property13. The Town of Kearney,
New Jersey holds an open lottery for parking permits 14. And the City of Grand Rapids (MI) offers
discounted permits according to financial need15.

Program Portability
While the details contained in the preceding document are largely specific to the proposed pilot
area, the general parameters of the proposed Residential Parking Permit (RPP) program are
portable and can be applied to other areas of the city within the following limitations;
 The maximum dimensions of any proposed pilot area should not exceed 1,200’ in width
or height. The proposed pilot area is roughly 1,200’ wide (east to west) at its furthermost
points and 1,000’ high (north to south). The next closest residential neighborhood to the
west40 measures roughly 1,100 x 1,100’ and could be a good candidate for another pilot.
 In contrast, the total area encompassing the existing overnight parking permit program
south of the Nashua River is almost 3,200’ high at its furthermost points and over 2,500’
wide. This area would need to be subdivided into as many as eight different zones in
order to maintain the walkability of each zone. Similarly, the streets with existing overnight
parking permit designations north of the Nashua River cover an area which is over half a
mile high and three-quarters of a mile wide and would need to be reorganized.
 Executing one or more pilots in the area between Walnut and Spring Street, the Nashua
River and West/ East Hollis Street will be exceptionally involved and complex in order to
balance the rights and needs of the residential community and the business community.
Similarly, any pilots which incorporate portions of West Hollis Street and Kinsley Street
south of the Nashua River or Canal Street north of the Nashua River will have similar
challenges.
